title: The girl who read Harry Potter first
hook: An eight-year-old's verdict helped get Harry Potter published.
peek: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone was turned down by about a dozen publishers. At Bloomsbury, the chairman took the opening chapter home to his young daughter, Alice, and her reaction helped tip the decision.
lede: In the mid-1990s, J.K. Rowling's agent sent the first Harry Potter book to publisher after publisher. About a dozen said no. When the manuscript reached the small children's list at Bloomsbury in London, the chairman, Nigel Newton, took the first chapter home to his eight-year-old daughter, Alice. She read it, then came back asking for the rest.

bullets.text: Alice was enthusiastic enough that her father later said her reaction was a key reason Bloomsbury took the book on. She wrote a short note saying it was one of the best books a child her age could read.
Bloomsbury paid an advance of about £2,500, a modest sum for a first novel. The editor Barry Cunningham reportedly told Rowling to get a day job, since children's books rarely made much money.
The Philosopher's Stone came out in 1997 with a first hardback run of only about 500 copies, many of which went to libraries. Those first-edition copies are now among the most valuable modern books.
The publishers worried that boys might not pick up a book by a woman, so they asked for initials. Rowling has no middle name, so she borrowed the K from her grandmother Kathleen.
